newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Retail sales, fed surveys due.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Retail sales, fed surveys due.

text.p: Bonds may break out of recent trading ranges on Tuesday as players get to see potentially market-moving data ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy-making meeting on May 20.

April retail sales will be reported at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT and economists expected they would be down 0.3 percent after a 0.1 percent rise in March. Fed policymakers will eye the number in an attempt to divine how strong the economy was.
Economists have said lean inventories should depress retail sales, even if growth wasn't slowing.
Still, many economists predicted strong growth and a tight labor market would prompt the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy at its next meeting.
"The news (on retial sales) ought to be friendly for the market. We expect them to be down because of weaker car sales," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Glassman said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments last Thursday indicated that slowing growth and moderating demand would leave leeway for the central bank to pause in tightening.
Strong retail sales seen earlier this year could have been aided by favorable weather and bonus payments, thus distorting the true strength of the numbers, Glassman said.
Trading volume was very light and prices were range bound late Monday ahead of Tuesday's data. But volume was expected to pick up considerably on Tuesday.

In addition to retail sales, the Atlanta Fed was scheduled to release its April index at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT along with the Richmond Fed's survey. Other sales indicators also would come with the BTM/Schroders index at 0900/1300 GMT and the Redbook reading at 1455 EDT/1855 GMT.

"It seems we're higher today based on expectations of a weaker number. So if we get a consensus or higher reading there's more downside than upside risk tomorrow," said Kathy Bostjancic, economist at UBS Securities Inc.
She said that risk was built in, as virtually all the forecast community was calling for weak retail sales numbers on Tuesday.
The high current capacity utilization rate and tight labor market still made the case for the Fed to tighten, Bostjancic said, even if sales were to slow.
